title: BRICS reaches for a crescendo
gist: At the September 2026 BRICS summit in Delhi, the 160-performer 'BRICS Symphony' used the European orchestra as a symbol of a multipolar order built on difference; the author argues this repurposing of an inherited form mirrors how 19th-century Russia absorbed European music, and that the image's ambiguity lets India stress diversity while Russian media spin it as anti-Western.

insights.claim: At the 2026 BRICS summit in Delhi, around 160 performers staged the 'BRICS Symphony – One Rhythm, Many Cultures' at Narendra Modi's gala dinner, combining instruments like Russia's balalaika and bayan with China's erhu and guzheng.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: Illustrates BRICS investing in soft-power cohesion signalling under India's chairmanship.

insights.claim: An orchestra is an effective symbol for BRICS because its symbolism is based on difference: members remain independent and recognisable yet coordination is possible, fitting a grouping with no shared history or political system.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: Frames BRICS as loose coordination rather than a bloc — temper expectations of unified BRICS economic action.
insights.quote: Its symbolism is based on difference. A violin does not need to turn into a flute for the ensemble to function.
insights.locator: How can a symbol of unity be created

insights.claim: Music works well as cultural diplomacy because, unlike political declarations requiring agreed wording, it can project harmony without defining what that harmony means.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: BRICS uses ambiguity to paper over divergent member interests; substantive agreements remain harder.
insights.quote: Music, however, can create an image of harmony without defining exactly what that harmony means.
insights.locator: This flexibility is a reason why music works

insights.claim: One Russian media outlet described the BRICS Symphony as a 'musical slap in the face to the West', while India's official framing stressed cultural diversity via 'One Rhythm, Many Cultures'.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: Same BRICS event carries opposite signals for different members; India resists an anti-Western framing.
insights.locator: The political flexibility of the performance

insights.claim: India prefers a multipolar order and worries about BRICS acquiring an explicitly anti-Western character, trying to keep a foot in multiple diplomatic camps rather than equating BRICS membership with alignment against the West.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: India acts as a brake on BRICS de-dollarisation/anti-Western moves; relevant for assessing BRICS currency or payments ambitions.
insights.locator: BRICS faces a more complex challenge

insights.claim: India makes extensive use of culture and identity in its foreign policy as part of Modi's diplomatic toolkit and a broader soft-power push.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: India's soft-power strategy is a durable feature of its diplomacy.
insights.locator: India already makes extensive use of culture

insights.claim: The modern orchestra is largely a product of European musical culture tied to royal courts, yet its political meaning is not permanently European; old forms acquire new meanings in new hands.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: BRICS need not invent a new cultural vocabulary; it co-opts Western forms, as it may with institutions.
insights.quote: Political orders rarely create their symbols from nothing; old forms can acquire completely different meanings in new hands.
insights.locator: There is, however, an intriguing historical irony

insights.claim: 19th-century Russia absorbed European musical traditions — founding the Russian Musical Society in 1859, St Petersburg Conservatoire in 1862 and Moscow Conservatoire in 1866 — and by century's end Russian music was itself a cultural export.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for non-Western powers adopting then exporting Western institutional forms.

insights.claim: Glinka's opera A Life for the Tsar (1836) exemplifies how borrowed European forms acquired distinctly national significance in Russia.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: Context only; supports the adaptation thesis.

insights.claim: BRICS may have less need to invent a new cultural vocabulary than its rhetoric about a changing world order suggests, because political power has always adapted inherited cultural forms.
insights.speaker: Stacy Jarvis
insights.so_what: Suggests BRICS' 'new order' is more evolutionary adaptation of existing structures than rupture.
insights.locator: A flag usually calls on the audience
